Network inference

Author

Mariam Rahali Masbouri

Published

March 22, 2026

In this file, we will perform network inference on the gut microbiota datasets using three different methods: LIMITS, FlashWeave and BEEM-Static. We will first import the relevant datasets from the dysbiotic cohorts (that is, those pertaining to IBD, IBS, CRC, and CDI) as well as the healthy cohorts from the Human Microbiome Project (HMPv13 and HMPv35), NIBIOHN and MORINAGA cohorts, and a “diet intervention” cohort as well. We describe first each tool and its implementation in the following sections, and then we will compare the results obtained from each method in a final section.

Importing the MAE object

Code 
mae_file <- 
  fs::dir_ls(str_c(data_dir(), "/02-processed-data"), regexp = "MAE_processed_.*\\.rds$") |> 
  sort(decreasing = TRUE) |>
  magrittr::extract(1)


cat(str_c("Loading MultiAssayExperiment from: 00_data/", mae_file |> str_remove(data_dir()), "\n"))
Loading MultiAssayExperiment from: 00_data//02-processed-data/MAE_processed_20260321.rds
Code 
mae <- readRDS(mae_file)

rm(mae_file)

mae
A MultiAssayExperiment object of 9 listed
 experiments with user-defined names and respective classes.
 Containing an ExperimentList class object of length 9:
 [1] IBD: SummarizedExperiment with 432 rows and 1630 columns
 [2] IBS: SummarizedExperiment with 598 rows and 62 columns
 [3] CDI: SummarizedExperiment with 868 rows and 366 columns
 [4] CRC: SummarizedExperiment with 837 rows and 575 columns
 [5] HMPV13: SummarizedExperiment with 660 rows and 171 columns
 [6] HMPV35: SummarizedExperiment with 1179 rows and 308 columns
 [7] NIBIOHN: SummarizedExperiment with 351 rows and 954 columns
 [8] MORINAGA: SummarizedExperiment with 281 rows and 642 columns
 [9] DIET: SummarizedExperiment with 193 rows and 114 columns
Functionality:
 experiments() - obtain the ExperimentList instance
 colData() - the primary/phenotype DataFrame
 sampleMap() - the sample coordination DataFrame
 `$`, `[`, `[[` - extract colData columns, subset, or experiment
 *Format() - convert into a long or wide DataFrame
 assays() - convert ExperimentList to a SimpleList of matrices
 exportClass() - save data to flat files

Network inference with LIMITS

In this section, we will apply LIMITS to the IBD cohort only (since it is the only cohort that has enough time points to apply the method).

IBD cohort

A sample (starting with H) has a taxon with relative abundance == 1.

We first import the IBD dataset from the MAE object in the chunk code below.

Code 
tmp <-
  mae[["IBD"]] |>
  assay() |>
  t() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("uid") |>
  pivot_longer(-uid, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "rel_ab") |>
  left_join(
    mae[["IBD"]] |> colData() |> as_tibble(rownames = "uid") |> select(uid, pid, visit_num, diagnosis),
    by = join_by(uid)
  )

Prevalence filtering

We will then filter out low-abundance taxa, by keeping only taxa that are present in at least 5% of the samples, and the remaining is grouped in a category named “Other”. This is done in the chunk code below.

Code 
tmp_healthy <- tmp |> filter(diagnosis == "nonIBD")
tmp_diseased <- tmp |> filter(diagnosis == "UC" | diagnosis == "CD")
Code 
# for healthy samples

tmp_filtered_healthy <- 
  filter_prevalence(tmp_healthy, prevalence_threshold = 0.05) |>
  left_join(
    mae[["IBD"]] |> colData() |> as.data.frame() |> as_tibble(rownames = "uid") |> 
      select(uid, pid, visit_num, diagnosis),
    by = join_by(uid)
  )
Keeping 145 out of 432 taxa with prevalence >= 5 %
Code 
# for diseased samples

tmp_filtered_diseased <- 
  filter_prevalence(tmp_diseased, prevalence_threshold = 0.05) |>
  left_join(
    mae[["IBD"]] |> colData() |> as.data.frame() |> as_tibble(rownames = "uid") |> 
      select(uid, pid, visit_num, diagnosis),
    by = join_by(uid)
  )
Keeping 143 out of 432 taxa with prevalence >= 5 %

  column_to_rownames("uid") |>
  t()
Code

diseased_df <-
  tmp_filtered_diseased |>
  select(uid, taxon, rel_ab) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = taxon, values_from = rel_ab) |>

We plot the results below.

Code 
# PEP plot

df_res |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = group, y = pep, color = group, fill = group) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.4, color = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1), alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Healthy" = "#0078B9", "Diseased" = "#EA0017")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = c("Healthy" = "#0078B9", "Diseased" = "#EA0017")) +
  facet_wrap(~ fraction) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Positive edge percentage (PEP)", color = "Group", fill = "Group") +
  stat_compare_means(
    comparisons = list(c("Healthy", "Diseased")),
    method = "wilcox.test",
    label = "p.signif",
    tip.length = 0.01,
    bracket.size = 0.8,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  
  df_res |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = group, y = sheldon, color = group, fill = group) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.4, color = NA) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1), alpha = 0.6) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Healthy" = "#0078B9", "Diseased" = "#EA0017")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = c("Healthy" = "#0078B9", "Diseased" = "#EA0017")) +
  facet_wrap(~ fraction) +
  labs(x = "", y = "Sheldon evenness", color = "Group", fill = "Group") +
  stat_compare_means(
    comparisons = list(c("Healthy", "Diseased")),
    method = "wilcox.test",
    label = "p.signif",
    tip.length = 0.01,
    bracket.size = 0.8,
    fontface = "bold"
  ) +
  
  patchwork::plot_layout(nrow = 2)

We will now check if there is any correlation between Sheldon eveness and PEP in the plot below.

Code 
df_res |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = sheldon, y = pep, color = group, fill = group) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE) +
  geom_smooth(aes(x = sheldon, y = pep), method = "lm",
              se = TRUE, inherit.aes = FALSE,
              color = "black", linetype = "dashed") +
  ggpubr::stat_cor(aes(label = after_stat(paste(r.label, p.label, sep = "~`,`~"))),
                   method = "pearson", label.x.npc = "left", label.y.npc = 0.12,
                   size = 3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  ggpubr::stat_cor(aes(x = sheldon, y = pep), method = "pearson",
                   inherit.aes = FALSE, color = "black",
                   label.x.npc = "left", label.y.npc = 0.03,
                   size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Healthy" = "#0078B9", "Diseased" = "#EA0017")) +
  scale_fill_manual(values  = c("Healthy" = "#0078B9", "Diseased" = "#EA0017")) +
  facet_wrap(~ fraction) +
  labs(x = "Sheldon evenness", y = "Positive edge percentage (PEP)", color = "Group", fill = "Group")

We will now perform the network analysis on top taxa selected based on their relative abundance. We select a data-driven threshold for relative abundance, which is shown in the plot below. We will keep taxa with a mean relative abundance of at least 0.001 (that is, log10 mean relative abundance of -3). This threshold correspond to the moment when the count starts to drop. Taxa with a mean relative abundance below this threshold will be grouped in a category named “Other”. This is done in the chunk code below.

Code 
# find data-driven threshold for relative abundance

tmp |>
  group_by(taxon) |>
  summarise(mean_rel_ab = mean(rel_ab)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_rel_ab)) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = mean_rel_ab |> log10()) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -3, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(x = "log10 mean relative abundance", y = "count",
       caption = "The vertical dashed red line indicates the selected threshold for mean relative abundance (0.001)")
Code 
# filter taxa based on mean relative abundance

tmp_filtered_healthy_top <- 
  filter_abundance(tmp_healthy, abundance_threshold = 0.001) |>
  left_join(
    mae[["IBD"]] |> colData() |> as_tibble(rownames = "uid") |> select(uid, pid, visit_num, diagnosis),
    by = join_by(uid)
  )
Keeping 74 out of 432 taxa with mean abundance >= 0.001
Code 
tmp_filtered_diseased_top <-
  filter_abundance(tmp_diseased, abundance_threshold = 0.001) |>
  left_join(
    mae[["IBD"]] |> colData() |> as_tibble(rownames = "uid") |> select(uid, pid, visit_num, diagnosis),
    by = join_by(uid)
  )
Keeping 80 out of 432 taxa with mean abundance >= 0.001

IBS cohort

Code 
tmp <-
  mae[["IBS"]] |> 
  assay() |> 
  t() |> 
  as.data.frame() |> 
  rownames_to_column("uid") |> 
  pivot_longer(-uid, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(uid) |>
  mutate(rel_ab = count/sum(count)) |>
  left_join(
    mae[["IBS"]] |> colData() |> as_tibble(rownames = "uid") |> select(uid, pid, time, cohort), 
    by = join_by(uid)
  )

tmp_diseased <- tmp |> filter(cohort == c("C", "D"))

Important

The IBS cohort has only 21 samples for the healthy cohorts, which is not sufficient to run FlashWeave with the selected parameters. A solution can be to modify the max_k parameter, at the cost of inflating the number of indirect edges.

We will now perform the network analysis on top taxa selected based on their relative abundance. We select a data-driven threshold for relative abundance, which is shown in the plot below. We will keep taxa with a mean relative abundance of at least 0.001 (that is, log10 mean relative abundance of -4). This threshold correspond to the moment when the count starts to drop. Taxa with a mean relative abundance below this threshold will be grouped in a category named “Other”. This is done in the chunk code below.

Code 
# find data-driven threshold for relative abundance

tmp |>
  group_by(taxon) |>
  summarise(mean_rel_ab = mean(rel_ab)) |>
  arrange(desc(mean_rel_ab)) |>
  ggplot() +
  aes(x = mean_rel_ab |> log10()) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -3, linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
  labs(x = "log10 mean relative abundance", y = "count",
       caption = "The vertical dashed red line indicates the selected threshold for mean relative abundance (0.00001)")

Network inference with BEEM-Static

In this section, we will apply BEEM-Static to the differents cohorts from the main analysis, and additionnaly compute beta diversity, evenness, and richness measures.

IBD cohort (Lloyd-Price et al. 2019)

A sample (starting with H) has a taxon with relative abundance == 1.

We first import the IBD dataset from the MAE object in the chunk code below.

Code 
tmp <-
  mae[["IBD"]] |>
  assay() |>
  t() |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("uid") |>
  pivot_longer(-uid, names_to = "taxon", values_to = "rel_ab") |>
  left_join(
    mae[["IBD"]] |> colData() |> as_tibble(rownames = "uid") |> select(uid, pid, visit_num, diagnosis),
    by = join_by(uid)
  )

Prevalence filtering

We will then filter out low-abundance taxa, by keeping only taxa that are present in at least 20% of the samples, and the remaining is grouped in a category named “Other”. This is done in the chunk code below.

Note

The choice of a prevalence threshold of 20% is somewhat arbitrary, but it is necessary in this case since BEEM-Static does not handle datasets with lots of zeros well.

Code
